blocks.x: So your original piano style and organ style would have been learned from your mother, you think?

Well now you didn't come here while you were in gospel this is... No, I'm not in gospel. No, no, you didn't know while he was in gospel. He didn't know. He traveled with the convention now. Convention? Well, you're probably one of the things that we need to make note here, and the reason that he has not gained the fame as he should have had, I mean, you know, all of the accolades, is because he has never been one to promote himself. You see, he never promoted himself. He always helped others, and it was those others who gained the fame. So now he has a promoter, okay, and he deserves to be promoted.

Well I came here with the National Baptist Convention, that's one of the biggest organizations in the country. Come here with him, played for him. Remember that? Remember that? He helped him to bring the musicians out, I mean, teach the musicians. And we'd start on that, and of course it didn't be very much for us. We'd start on that three or four weeks before convention time. Getting these folk together, they couldn't all come to the same place, but they're scattered all over the country. You'd go to here, to this one tonight, go to somebody the next night, or somebody out of town the next night, and then when you get them all in, when you got down to the big meetings, you had them all put them together. They'd do stuff that's all. It's just that easy, if you knew how to do it.
Did you know a New Orleans gospel singer, Bessie Griffin? Bessie Griffin? Yeah, I knew. Is she still living?

Yeah, she's in California, out in Los Angeles now. Oh, she's out in Los Angeles. Remember she came to Chicago, remember Mahalia brought her to Chicago, and remember when we had the convention there in Chicago, Mahalia called, there were four great black gospel singers, women. One was Willa May Ford Smith, one was Bessie Griffin, one was Janice Jones, Ernestine Washington out of New York, and Mahalia. They were the top five divas of gospel music in the early days, and she was one of those. She was one of those.
She was one of those. Yeah. Did you see anything in similarity between Mahalia style and Bessie Griffin style at the time?

Well, for so, I didn't pay any attention. When one had the floor, I was on that floor, I was giving them all the credit. What we're trying to get at is, was there anything about these New Orleans singers that really made them different?

Bessie and Mahalia style was similar. Uh-huh. In fact, they were a take off of Bessie Smith. Uh-huh. Yeah. Both styles, Mahalia and Bessie, they were almost identical. And then, but there was a man also, two men, who also had that same style that did not come from New Orleans, you see. There was Brother Joe May, and Cleophus Robinson. Uh-huh. All their styles are all similar. Oh, yeah. Mm-hmm. It's all similar, you see. But it was Mahalia who made it famous. Well, Mahalia covered the whole world.

Mahalia not only, she worked in everything, just the church, the lodge, wherever they wanted her to sing, and she sang her gospel songs, she was easy to get. And she loved to do it. Now the boy you just mentioned there, he's good, but he didn't get around as much as Mahalia.
You mean Joe May or Cleopas?
Either one of the hands.
Cleopas and John.

Yeah. Yeah. They were like Mahalia. In fact, they couldn't. Yeah. Mahalia had a style that they couldn't even emulate. So, one thing that hurt me most, other than anything in life, except my mom can't believe God, when I heard that Mahalia's dead, I didn't know what to do. I didn't know what to do. I wouldn't go home, wouldn't go to die, I think. I went to a funeral. You did it, yeah. I didn't want to see it. Well, she does not another Mahalia Jackson.
You may never. Well, you know, she recorded a whole album of just your songs.
Their own songs?
Yeah, just her songs, Dorsey's songs. Yeah. That was a tribute to him. And the great friendships that she had for her.
To take another tack regarding New Orleans music, did you know other musicians, particularly in your blues days, that came from New Orleans? In Chicago, for example, did you know Tony Jackson?
Yeah, I know Tony. And you have to name him. I can tell you by the name. I forgot.
Did you know any of the jazz players that came up from New Orleans in the early twenties, like Joe Oliver?
Yeah, Joe Oliver. I did, I know him. I played the same cabaret. He did.
Did you tell us anything about him? Anything that comes back to mind? No, I couldn't, but he's a little bit beyond me. Yeah. All I could do, hey Joe, how you doing?
He's gone. He's gone. He's a bigger man. He might not have seen you. He was called Bad Eyes in the stuff. Did you know Louis? Yeah, Joe was great.
Yeah, Joe was great. Yeah, Joe was great.

segments.title: Dorsey and the National Baptist Convention; why he never promoted himself
segments.summary: Asked about his piano and organ style, the companion says Dorsey never promoted himself and helped others gain fame. Dorsey describes coming with the National Baptist Convention and preparing musicians for weeks beforehand.

segments.title: Bessie Griffin and the top gospel divas
segments.summary: Asked about New Orleans gospel singer Bessie Griffin, the companion says she is now in Los Angeles, was brought to Chicago by Mahalia, and was one of the five top gospel divas.

segments.title: Mahalia Jackson's style, comparisons, her death and her Dorsey album
segments.summary: The companion compares Mahalia's and Bessie Griffin's styles, and those of Joe May and Cleophus Robinson. Dorsey praises Mahalia's reach, describes his grief at her death, and the companion mentions her album of his songs.

segments.title: Chicago blues-era New Orleans players: Tony Jackson and Joe Oliver
segments.summary: Dorsey says he knew Tony Jackson and Joe Oliver, with whom he played the same cabaret; Oliver was a bigger man who might not notice him.
